title: Neuromuscular Weakness: Myasthenia Gravis, Guillain–Barré & Respiratory Crisis
html:
Neuromuscular disease can cause life-threatening respiratory failure while the patient remains awake and the pulse oximeter still looks normal. Myasthenia gravis (MG) impairs neuromuscular-junction signaling and often causes fluctuating, fatigable weakness. Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy that can progress over days with limb, bulbar, respiratory, and autonomic involvement. The RN must repeatedly assess strength, breathing mechanics, cough, swallowing, and the trend—not simply wait for hypoxemia.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate typical MG and GBS patterns without assuming either diagnosis from one symptom.
  • Identify impending respiratory or airway compromise before oxygen saturation falls.
  • Support ordered MG crisis treatment and GBS immune therapy while monitoring safety.
  • Recognize GBS-related autonomic instability and common immobility complications.
  • Plan medication timing, swallowing protection, rehabilitation, and patient education.

Compare the patterns

MG may begin with ptosis or diplopia and cause speech change, chewing fatigue, dysphagia, weak neck flexion, or proximal limb weakness. Symptoms can worsen with activity and improve after rest; sensation and deep-tendon reflexes are usually preserved. Infection, surgery, heat, stress, missed therapy, and some medications can worsen weakness. A stable-looking patient who is newly unable to finish a sentence or clear secretions may be approaching myasthenic crisis.

GBS often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection and typically produces rapidly progressive bilateral limb weakness with diminished or absent reflexes and possible paresthesias or pain. Progression may reach facial, swallowing, or respiratory muscles. Do not insist on a perfectly symmetric ascending pattern before considering GBS; variants exist. Autonomic dysfunction may cause abrupt blood-pressure fluctuations, tachycardia or bradycardia, arrhythmias, sweating changes, or urinary retention. Cerebrospinal fluid and nerve-conduction studies can support diagnosis but may be less definitive early; a worsening bedside examination demands action even while testing continues.

Respiratory surveillance: oxygen saturation can be late

Assess work and pattern of breathing, ability to speak full sentences, orthopnea, head or neck strength, cough effectiveness, secretion control, swallowing, respiratory rate, and mental status. Follow ordered serial forced vital capacity (FVC), negative inspiratory force (NIF) or maximal inspiratory pressure, and single-breath count where used. Trend the results and patient together; no single cutoff replaces clinical judgment. In both MG and GBS, a weak cough or bulbar dysfunction can threaten airway protection before blood gas or pulse oximetry becomes abnormal. New rapid shallow breathing, paradoxical breathing, weak neck flexion, inability to lie flat, drooling, or falling respiratory measurements calls for urgent respiratory and critical-care review.

Prepare airway equipment and suction, position for comfort and secretion management, maintain aspiration precautions, and avoid delaying escalation for repeat measurements when the patient is visibly tiring. Oxygen may correct hypoxemia but cannot restore weak ventilation. Noninvasive ventilation may be appropriate for selected patients who can protect the airway and clear secretions; progressive bulbar weakness, aspiration risk, or inadequate ventilation may require intubation. The team makes airway decisions early enough to avoid a crash airway.

Myasthenia gravis: recognize crisis and use medicines safely

A myasthenic crisis is severe MG-related weakness threatening ventilation or airway protection. Infection and medication changes are common triggers. Assess fever and infection, recent surgery, treatment interruptions, new antibiotics or other drugs that can worsen MG, and the patient's usual bulbar and respiratory baseline. Avoid automatically increasing pyridostigmine for every episode of weakness; excessive cholinesterase-inhibitor exposure can cause more secretions, gastrointestinal symptoms, and other adverse effects, and the plan may change during ventilation. The neurologist directs medication adjustments.

Pyridostigmine is a symptomatic therapy for many patients with MG. When ordered for oral intake, schedule it as directed in relation to meals so chewing and swallowing strength is useful at mealtime; verify swallowing safety and never force an oral dose into an unsafe airway. Long-term immunotherapy and thymectomy are selected by the specialist for the MG subtype and individual patient. Impending or established crisis may require ICU care plus IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange (PLEX) as directed. These treatments do not replace immediate respiratory support. Monitor IVIG for infusion reactions, renal or volume problems, and thrombosis risk; monitor PLEX access, blood pressure, bleeding and electrolyte concerns under protocol.

Guillain–Barré: immune treatment and autonomic monitoring

GBS can worsen quickly even when initial leg weakness appears mild. Record serial limb and neck strength, reflexes, walking ability, facial and bulbar function, cough and FVC or other ordered respiratory measures. Use continuous or frequent cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring when autonomic instability is suspected. Report marked heart-rate or blood-pressure swings, dysrhythmia, urinary retention, severe pain, or new swallowing difficulty promptly.

Current EAN/PNS guidance supports IVIG or PLEX for appropriately selected patients with significant GBS; the specialist chooses treatment based on severity, timing, comorbidities, and access. Routine corticosteroids are not an effective GBS disease treatment, and immediate sequential PLEX plus IVIG is not routinely recommended. Follow the ordered infusion or exchange safety plan. Prevent pressure injury, falls, venous thromboembolism, constipation, urinary problems, contractures, and anxiety with individualized care. Provide pain management and PT, OT, speech or swallow, and rehabilitation support as the patient stabilizes. Recovery can be prolonged; communicate realistic milestones rather than promising rapid full strength.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Compare ptosis, diplopia, fatigability, limb weakness, reflexes, speech, swallowing, cough, breathing, vital signs, and respiratory-measure trends with baseline.
  2. Analyze cues: MG suggests fluctuating neuromuscular-junction weakness; GBS suggests progressive peripheral weakness with reflex and autonomic findings, but diagnostic testing and specialist review are needed.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway loss, hypoventilation, aspiration, severe dysautonomia, and rapidly progressive weakness outrank routine mobility or discharge tasks.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare respiratory support and monitoring, safe swallowing plan, ordered IVIG or PLEX, medication review, and complication prevention.
  5. Take action: Escalate early, support airway and secretion clearance, perform serial ordered assessments, give therapy safely, and communicate trend changes precisely.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm stable ventilation, cough and swallowing, strength and functional trajectory, hemodynamics, treatment tolerance, and rehabilitation needs.

Clinical example

A client with MG is admitted for infection and new difficulty swallowing. At first, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Two hours later, speech is weaker, the client cannot clear secretions, and serial FVC is falling. The RN recognizes impending respiratory failure despite the normal saturation, stops oral intake, calls the emergency and neurology teams, prepares suction and airway support, and reports the exact strength and breathing trend. Waiting for the saturation to fall could make airway management dangerously late.
